newsitem.title: CHILE: Seaweed, not sabotage, caused Chilean blackout.
newsitem.headline: Seaweed, not sabotage, caused Chilean blackout.

text.p: A blackout that plunged nearly all of Chile into darkness on Thursday night was not the work of May Day guerrilla bombers, as many Chileans feared, but rather a much more slippery foe: seaweed.

Chile's largest electrical utility Endesa said on Friday that a large amount of marine kelp slipped into cooling ducts at a seaside power plant, shutting the plant down and casting 93 percent of Chile's population into darkness.

The blackout began at about 11:30 p.m. on Thursday night (0330 GMT on Friday) and lasted about half an hour, turning traffic in Santiago into chaos, alarming police and throwing computers out of whack.

Since it occurred on May 1 -- which, as International Workers' Day is a common date for bombings and demonstrations by left-wing rebel groups in Latin America -- many Chileans assumed the blackout was the work of such a group.

"In fact, what happened was that marine kelp was introduced into the ducts, provoking a problem in the plant," Endesa's commercial manager Juan Eduardo Vasquez told reporters. The company had ruled out sabotage as the cause of the blackout, Endesa officials said.

The blackout affected all of Chile from the northern town of Taltal to the southern port of Ancud, an area covering 80 percent of the country's energy consumption and 93 percent of its population, Endesa officials said.
